To express purpose with per + infinitive when the subject is the same: Studio per capire.
To use affinché / perché + subjunctive when the subject changes.
To apply the sequence of tenses: L’ho detto perché lo sapesse.
To use in modo che / così che + subjunctive.
To use pur di + infinitive: Pur di vederla, farei qualsiasi cosa.
To tell "perché" of cause (indicative) from "perché" of purpose (subjunctive).
Florence, early May. Matei and Giulia are back from Sicily. In the workshop, they present a new project to Professor Bellini.
Professor, we'd like to open the workshop to the public on Saturday mornings, so that people can see how the work is done.
Open the workshop? So that people can come and touch the paintings?
No, Professor. We'll put up a glass panel so that nobody can touch anything.
Hmm. And for what purpose, exactly?
To make young people understand that paintings don't restore themselves. Like in Syracuse. There, the whole city mobilised so that the restoration could continue.
Syracuse… All right. But for it to work, you need someone to explain. I haven't got the patience.
Pietro has volunteered. He'd do anything just to come to the workshop.
Eleven in July. And he knows Ernesto's rule better than any of us.
Then let's write the rule on the door, so that everyone reads it on the way in.
Exactly. But add underneath, in small letters: "Then, if you like, come back." So that they come back. That's the point, isn't it?
Double FF, stress at the end: af-feen-KAY.
When the person doing the main action is also the one with the aim, use PER + INFINITIVE (like English "to / in order to"):
I'm learning Italian to work in Florence.
We're putting up a glass panel to protect the painting.
After verbs of motion (andare, venire, uscire) "a" is often used instead of "per": "Vado a vedere", "Vieni a mangiare".
When the aim concerns SOMEONE ELSE, use AFFINCHÉ or PERCHÉ + SUBJUNCTIVE:
We're opening the workshop so that people can see.
We're writing the rule so that everyone reads it.
I'm leaving you the keys so that you can get in.
Don't use the infinitive when the subject changes: NOT "Apriamo il laboratorio per la gente vedere". You say "affinché la gente veda".
If the main verb is in the past, the subjunctive moves to the imperfetto:
4. In modo che, così che, pur di
Mettiamo un vetro in modo che nessuno tocchi.
Scriviamola sulla porta, così che tutti la leggano.
Pur di venire, farebbe qualsiasi cosa.
allo scopo di / al fine di
Al fine di proteggere il quadro, …
"Pur di" shows you're ready for any sacrifice: "Pur di non lavare i piatti, Pietro fa i compiti." (Anything to avoid washing up — Pietro does his homework.)
"Perché" has two meanings. The mood of the verb shows which:
(I'm speaking quietly because Viola is asleep.)
(I'm speaking quietly so that Viola will sleep.)
Watch the difference! One letter changes the meaning: "dorme" (she's already asleep) / "dorma" (I want her to sleep).

On the first open Saturday twelve people came: three German tourists looking for the Uffizi, an elderly lady from the neighbourhood who just wanted to see "where Ernesto's grandson worked", a teacher with six children and two art students. Pietro, wearing a tie Graziella had made him put on so that he'd look more serious, welcomed them at the door and read the sign aloud: "Look. And don't touch anything. Then, if you like, come back."

Then he led them along the glass, explaining everything with a seriousness that made Giulia smile. "This is a scalpel. It's for removing old varnish, but only if you're very, very good. This is a microscope, for looking at the colours close up. And this," he said, pointing at Matei, "is a restorer. He's for repairing paintings, but you mustn't disturb him while he works, so that he doesn't make mistakes." The children laughed, and so did the Germans, who hadn't understood a word.

Graziella, of course, couldn't just stand and watch. On the second Saturday she put a little table outside the workshop door, with a thermos of coffee and a tray of schiacciata, and a sign: "Pay what you like, to buy materials". Just so as not to lose their place in front of the glass, people bought coffee and drank it standing in the queue. At the end of the month, with Graziella's donations, Matei bought a new microscope, so that the children could look through it too.

On the second Saturday there were forty people. On the third, after a local paper had run an article called "The workshop that opens its doors", the queue stretched all the way to the bridge. Bellini, who had said he wanted nothing to do with the project, came down every Saturday "to make sure nobody touched anything", and then stayed all morning answering questions, with his hands behind his back.

It was on that third Saturday that Giulia noticed the boy. He was twelve or thirteen, with short black hair and a rucksack too big for him. He didn't ask questions. He didn't talk to anyone. He just stood in front of the glass, motionless, watching Matei work on a small fifteenth-century Madonna. When the visit was over and everyone had left, he stayed there, until Pietro politely told him they had to close.

The next Saturday he came back. And the one after that. He always arrived first, always left last, and never said a word. Just to stay a few minutes longer, he helped Pietro tidy away the chairs. One morning Giulia brought him a glass of water and asked him his name. "Davide," he said, so quietly that she had to lean down to hear. He lived in San Frediano, two streets from the workshop. His mother was a nurse and worked night shifts at the hospital.

It was Bellini, though, who understood first. One Saturday he went up to the boy, who as usual was looking through the glass, and asked him, without any preamble: "Do you draw?" Davide went red. He hesitated for a long time, then opened his rucksack and took out an exercise book. It was full of drawings: the Madonnas in the workshop, Matei's hands, the brushes, the microscope, even Bellini's profile with his hands behind his back. They were extraordinary drawings, precise and full of light.

Bellini leafed through the book in silence, page after page, for ten minutes. Then he closed it and handed it back to the boy. "Where did you learn?" "By myself," said Davide. "By looking." Bellini nodded slowly. Matei and Giulia, on the other side of the glass, stopped working. They had seen that expression on the professor's face only once before: the day he had talked about his grandfather Ernesto.

That evening Bellini went to talk to Davide's mother, a tired, kind woman who listened to him standing at her front door, still in her nurse's uniform. He suggested that the boy come to the workshop every Saturday, not as a visitor but as an apprentice, so that he could learn the craft at close quarters. Free of charge, of course. "Why are you doing this?" she asked, wary. "You don't even know us."

Bellini thought for a moment. Then he said: "Madam, in 1966, when I was two, my grandfather used to take me to work because my mother was ill. He taught me to look. Now I'm about to retire, and I have no children or grandchildren. I'm doing it so that what my grandfather taught me isn't lost." The woman looked at him for a long time. Then she called her son: "Davide! Come here. The gentleman wants to talk to you."

That night Davide didn't sleep. He filled three pages of his exercise book with drawings of brushes, hands, eyes. His mother, coming home from her shift at dawn, found him asleep on the kitchen table with the pencil still in his hand. She didn't wake him. She put a blanket over his shoulders, looked at the drawings for a long time and, for the first time in many months, smiled.

The following Saturday Davide arrived at eight, an hour before opening. Bellini was waiting for him behind the glass, on the restorers' side. He took a small brush from the drawer, one of his own, with a worn handle, and put it in his hand. Then he said the words his grandfather had said to him sixty years earlier, which Matei and Giulia knew by heart: "Look. And don't touch anything."

That evening, in his study, Bellini opened a new notebook, black, just like his grandfather's. On the first page he wrote in his elegant hand: "Workshop diary. Saturday, 6th June. Today an apprentice arrived. His name is Davide. He is twelve years old and he already knows how to look." Then he closed the notebook, switched off the light and, for the first time since he had decided to retire, didn't feel old.

Pietro, on the other side of the glass, was watching the scene with a touch of jealousy. Giulia went over to him. "Are you cross?" Pietro thought about it. "A bit," he admitted. "But it's fine. I'll be the guide, and he'll be the restorer. That way, when he's famous, I'll tell everyone it was me who let him in the first time." Giulia hugged him. Pietro was nearly eleven, and sometimes he talked like Bellini.
